chapters.title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
chapters.author: Sudha Murty
chapters.overview: The narrator recalls how, at twelve, she read the Kannada serial Kashi Yatre aloud every week to her grandmother Krishtakka, who had never gone to school. When the narrator was away for a week, her grandmother could not read the episode and felt dependent and helpless, so at sixty-two she resolved to learn the Kannada alphabet by Saraswati Puja. She worked hard, learned to read, and at Dassara touched the feet of her granddaughter as her teacher. The unit also contains the poem 'Bharat Our Land' by Subramania Bharati.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Asks why it is important to learn how to read and write, with a word web to complete.
Questions about the languages grandparents speak, how they spend time and favourite experiences with them.
A passage in which highlighted words (protagonist, debate, episode, community, concentration, eagerly, convincing, guided) are matched with meanings.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: Part I: at about twelve the narrator lives with her grandparents in a village in north Karnataka, where papers and magazines arrive late.
The Kannada writer Triveni's novel Kashi Yatre, about an old lady who gives her savings for an orphan girl's wedding instead of going to Kashi, appears as a serial in the weekly Karmaveera.
The narrator reads each episode to her grandmother Krishtakka, who never went to school, identifies with the protagonist and discusses it with friends.
Returning after a week at a wedding, the narrator finds her grandmother in tears; at night Avva tells her how she lost her mother, married young and never went to school.
Part II: Avva explains she could not read the episode, felt dependent and helpless, and decides to learn the Kannada alphabet with Saraswati Puja day during Dassara as the deadline.

The narrator laughs at first, but Avva says 'For learning there is no age bar', studies hard, and at Dassara touches her teacher's feet; she reads the title of the gift, Kashi Yatre, and passes 'with flying colours'.

sections.title: Check Your Understanding
points: After Part I: a cause and effect table, whether the narrator expected to see her grandmother in tears, and how she might help her.
After Part II: true or false statements about the grandmother's reasons for learning, her belief that there is no age limit, and her respect for the narrator as a teacher.

sections.title: Critical Reflection
points: Extract-based questions on the grandmother's tears, the tender atmosphere, and her determination to be independent.

Questions on why she felt embarrassed to ask others, why the narrator laughed, the significance of Kashi Yatre, the lesson of touching the narrator's feet, and the value of education for independence.

sections.title: Bharat Our Land

It celebrates the mighty Himavant, the generous Ganga, the sacred Upanishads, gallant warriors, sages, divine music, Brahma-knowledge and the Buddha's dhamma, with the refrain 'she's peerless, let's praise her!'

subsections.title: Critical Reflection

chapters.title: The Pot Maker
chapters.author: Temsula Ao
chapters.overview: Sentila dreams of becoming a pot maker like her mother Arenla and grandmother, but Arenla, worn down by the labour and poor returns of pottery, wants her to weave. After the village council reminds the family that a traditional skill belongs to no individual, Arenla teaches Sentila, but the girl cannot shape a pot until Onula, the kind dormitory warden, helps her and tells her to watch her mother. One day Sentila makes a batch almost equal to her mother's, and finds Arenla dead; Onula sees the two identical rows of pots and knows a new pot maker was born. The unit also contains the poem 'Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations'.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Identifying vocations from pictures and listing more.
Discussing what the pictures share, the word 'vocations', and differences between handmade and machine-made products.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: Part I: Sentila secretly learns by watching expert potters, because her mother Arenla says pot making brings only a pittance for exhausting work and wants her to weave.
Sentila observes how clay is pounded, shaped with the left hand and a spatula, dried and fired in a kiln.
Village gossip leads the council to summon her father Mesoba; the elders remind him that skills like pot making symbolise the people's tradition, belong to no individual, and must be passed on.
Part II: Arenla takes Sentila to the riverbank to dig clay and teaches her for a year, but Sentila cannot shape a pot.
In the girls' dormitory, Onula (Aunty) sees her tense efforts, shows her how to make a pot and tells her to watch how her mother shapes the mouth.

One sunny day Arenla leaves Sentila to work; Sentila makes pot after pot, one short of her mother's tally, then finds Arenla dead. Onula sees two identical rows of pots and realises 'A new pot maker was born.'

sections.title: Check Your Understanding
points: After Part I: whether pot making is easy, whether Sentila will fulfil her dream, and whether her parents will support her.
After Part II: whether Onula's support helped, what Sentila's observing tells us, and arranging the story's events in sequence.

sections.title: Critical Reflection
points: Extract questions on Arenla's reasons for preferring weaving and the word 'handsome', and on Onula's help and the word 'fashioned'.
Questions on the pot making process, the council's warning, Sentila's failure, Onula absorbing 'a new phenomenon', tradition belonging to no individual, the last line, and perseverance.

subsections.title: Quality
points: An abridged story by John Galsworthy about Mr Gessler, a German bootmaker in London who makes only what is ordered and whose boots never fail to fit.
He resents big firms that win trade by advertisement, not work; his elder brother dies and he grows old and worn.
His last boots are the best he ever made; soon after, he is dead of slow starvation, having spent everything on rent and leather — 'he made good boots.'

sections.title: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations

It celebrates craftspersons, artisans with lutes, carpenters, electricians, boatmen, shoemakers, the cook, designer and mason, each celebrating what belongs to them.
'The voice of their vocation is the voice of their identity.'

chapters.title: Winds of Change
chapters.overview: An informative piece on the pankha, the traditional Indian hand fan. It traces the word to 'pankh' (feather), notes evidence of fans in the Ajanta paintings and their use in temples and royal courts, and describes regional varieties made of distinct materials and designs in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Bihar and among tribes. It warns that technology threatens the craft, now largely decorative and commercial, and argues for celebrating pankhas and holding workshops to preserve it. The unit also contains the poem 'Canvas of Soil' by Maya Anthony.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Whether anyone at home uses a hand fan, what it is called and made of.
Completing information about fans from Assam, Kerala and Uttar Pradesh.
Matching words such as indigenous, innovative, industrious, intricate, invoked and initiatives with meanings.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: Pankha comes from 'pankh', feather of a bird; pankhi denotes a small plumed fan seen in Buddhist wall paintings at Ajanta from the 2nd century CE.
Pankhas fanned deities in temples and kings in courts, ranged from two inches to arm-sized, and became cultural goods on trade routes, with each region developing its own materials and designs.
Rajasthan has appliqué, zardozi, engraved brass temple and painted fans; Gujarat has cotton fans with mirror work, beads fans and Kutch's leather fans.

Bengal makes sola fans and palm leaf Tal Patar Pankha; Uttar Pradesh has Phadh fans; Odisha has palm leaf fans and Bihar bamboo fans; tribes use grass, cane, palm, geometric patterns and white-on-red designs.
With technology the culture of pankhas risks disappearing; now decorative and commercial, it provides some livelihood, and celebrating pankhas and holding workshops can preserve the craft.

sections.title: Check Your Understanding

sections.title: Critical Reflection
points: Extract questions on pankhas as cultural goods, fact and opinion, and assertion and reason; and on technology, commercialisation and livelihood.
Questions on the title 'Winds of Change', pankhas as testimony to regional identity, balancing tradition and innovation, workshops, and the changing cultural role of fans.

Reading O. Henry's story 'The Last Leaf'.

subsections.title: The Last Leaf
points: An abridged story by O. Henry: the young artist Johnsy, ill with pneumonia, believes she will die when the last ivy leaf outside her window falls.
Her friend Sue tells the old painter Behrman, whose dream is to paint a masterpiece.
The last leaf survives two storms; Johnsy regains the will to live.
Behrman dies of pneumonia; he had painted the leaf on the wall on the stormy night — his masterpiece.

sections.title: Canvas of Soil
points: A poem by Maya Anthony comparing a garden to a painting: earth is the palette, seeds are brushstrokes, blossoms a painted sight, and each plot a canvas.
'Where art and life coincide' — in the hands of those who till, gardens become paintings still.
The book suggests the poem may be read as an allegory of life's journey and growth, and of harmony and diversity.

subsections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Discussing what one sees in a garden, similarities between a garden and a painting, and the meanings of palette, hue and canvas.

subsections.title: Reading for Appreciation
points: The text of the poem.

subsections.title: Check Your Understanding
points: Completing stanza summaries, choosing stanza titles, and matching imagery, metaphor, rhyme scheme (AABB), tone, mood, speaker and alliteration with examples; allegory explained.

subsections.title: Critical Reflection
points: Extract questions on 'Brushstrokes of seeds', 'hue', 'Each plot, a canvas wide'; reasons for the comparisons; and questions on imagery, timelessness and the title.

subsections.title: Vocabulary in Context
points: Names of shades of blue, green and red, and painting-related words such as easel, tonal range, portrait, underpainting and mural.

subsections.title: Listen and Respond

subsections.title: Speaking Activity

subsections.title: Writing Task

subsections.title: Learning Beyond the Text
points: A mini-project on famous gardens, garden-inspired art, designing a garden or interviewing a gardener; reading Toru Dutt's poem.

sections.title: A Sea of Foliage Girds Our Garden Round
points: A sonnet-length poem by Toru Dutt describing a garden ringed by foliage of contrasting colours: tamarinds, mango clumps, palms and red seemuls.
Loveliest are the bamboos when the moon looks through and turns the white lotus into a cup of silver, like a primeval Eden.

keyResults.statement: The structure and design of pankhas reflect the cultural core of the region that crafts them, and the craft needs celebration and support to survive technological change.

keyResults.label: Regional pankhas

keyResults.label: Poetic devices in 'Canvas of Soil'
keyResults.statement: Imagery, metaphor (seeds as brushstrokes, plot as canvas), AABB rhyme scheme, alliteration ('Blossoms bloom'), an appreciative tone and joyful mood, with a gardener as speaker.

keyResults.label: Character (The Last Leaf): Behrman
keyResults.statement: A sixty-year-old painter who never painted his masterpiece until he painted the last leaf to save Johnsy.

chapters.title: Vitamin-M
chapters.author: Asha Nehemiah
chapters.overview: Ravi's seventy-five-year-old grandfather, a former lawyer, has come to live with the family in the city after a fall, and Ravi's mother, who thinks his memory is failing, tells Ravi never to let him go out alone. When Grandpa goes out, Ravi secretly follows him through a series of embarrassing mishaps, only to lose him to a stranger wearing Grandpa's cap. Grandpa is home asleep when Ravi returns; at dinner he reminds his daughter that she forgot his birthday, suggests she needs 'Vitamin-M', and gives Ravi a book of detective stories, with a twinkle that suggests he knew he was followed. The unit also contains the poem 'I Cannot Remember My Mother' by Rabindranath Tagore.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: A graphic organiser on caring for the elderly: their problems, reasons and how to care for them.
A vocabulary table for frail, shuddered, poky, forbid, pottering and winced.
Sharing a tradition, story or recipe passed down by grandparents.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: Part I: Ravi's mother Vidya wishes someone would invent a memory vitamin, 'Vitamin-M', for old people; Grandpa had taken a double dose of medicine and got lost once.
Grandpa, who kept house alone for ten years after his wife died, resents being brought from his quiet brick house to a 'poky little flat' and being forbidden to go out alone.
Grandpa plays a cunning game of chess and remembers famous games; he sets off to fetch the Tamil newspaper, and Ravi decides to follow him secretly.
Part II: Ravi is scolded by a mother in the park and by loud vendors under a banyan tree while Grandpa eats peanuts, sugary tea, bananas and ice cream.
Grandpa enters a barber shop; Ravi is thrown out of a ladies' salon, then chases a bus only to find a stranger wearing Grandpa's yellow cap, given to him by 'a kind old gentleman'.

Part III: Frantic, Ravi returns home to find Grandpa asleep; Grandpa tells Vidya that Ravi disappeared, gives everyone gifts on his own birthday, which Vidya forgot, says she needs Vitamin-M, and gives Ravi The Best Detective Stories.

sections.title: Check Your Understanding
points: After Part I: why Grandpa disliked the city, why Vidya did not want him out alone, and whether Ravi could keep his promise.
After Part II: a flow chart of Grandpa's day out, and whether he was really lost.
After Part III: Ravi's feelings on finding Grandpa, the significance of Grandpa's birthday gifts and the detective book.

sections.title: Critical Reflection
points: Extract questions on Grandpa's longing for his house in town, and on his cool reply and the gift parcel.
Questions on evidence that Grandpa's memory is not failing, character traits, whether Ravi is a good detective, who needs Vitamin-M, and age bias.

sections.title: Vocabulary and Structures in Context
points: Classifying movement and sound words (pottering, boomed, crouch, whirr) and using them in a detective passage.
Synonyms for 'dilemma', a word table, and matching emotions and expressions with meanings.
Prepositions of direction, location, time or manner.

A presentation on a personal experience of caring for an older person.

Reading Mulk Raj Anand's story 'The Lost Child'.

subsections.title: The Lost Child
points: A story by Mulk Raj Anand: at a spring festival fair a child keeps wanting toys, burfi, a garland and balloons, but moves on knowing his parents will refuse.
Asking to ride the roundabout, he finds his parents gone and runs in panic through the crowd.
A kind man rescues him and offers the ride, music, a balloon, a garland and sweets, but the child only sobs, 'I want my mother, I want my father!'

sections.title: I Cannot Remember My Mother
points: A poem by Rabindranath Tagore: the poet cannot remember his mother, but a tune she hummed while rocking his cradle hovers over his playthings.
The smell of shiuli flowers and the scent of the morning temple service come to him as her scent.
Looking at the distant blue sky, he feels the stillness of her gaze has spread all over the sky.

subsections.title: Reflect and Respond

subsections.title: Critical Reflection
points: Extract questions on the hovering tune and on the mother's gaze spreading over the sky; questions on the refrain, shiuli flowers, nature and the mother–child relationship.

chapters.title: The World of Limitless Possibilities
chapters.overview: After introducing the Paralympic Games and India's record in them, the chapter presents an interview with Dr. Deepa Malik, India's first female Paralympic medallist. Paralysed waist down after surgery for a spine tumour at 29, she chose to transform her life, took up para-athletics and won silver in shot-put at the 2016 Rio Paralympics. She speaks about overcoming societal perceptions, 'ability beyond disability', her advocacy for inclusivity, and her belief that disability is a unique strength waiting to be unleashed. The unit also contains the poem 'Nine Gold Medals' by David Roth.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: The Paralympic Games celebrate the resilience and talent of athletes with locomotor, sensory or intellectual disabilities; India debuted in 1968 and won its first medal, in swimming, in 1972.
Dr. Deepa Malik, a Khel Ratna, Arjuna and Padma Shri awardee, is named by the International Paralympic Committee among the 10 most inspirational women para-athletes.
Diagnosed with a spine tumour at 29 and paralysed waist down after surgery, she chose between squandering her life in remorse and a world of limitless possibilities, and switched to para-athletics.
Her breakthrough was a silver medal in shot-put at the 2016 Rio Paralympics; she is India's first female Paralympic medallist and first female para-athlete to win an Asian Games medal in athletics.

She overcame societal perceptions with mental resilience and family support, believes sports challenge stereotypes, and advocates for disability rights, women's empowerment through sports, and awareness in schools and colleges.
Her advice: every setback is an opportunity to prove your strength; disability is not a limitation but a unique strength waiting to be unleashed.

chapters.title: Twin Melodies
chapters.author: Mitra Phukan
chapters.overview: A three-act play about Shruti Sharma, a young violinist who secretly rehearses with a fusion group while her father, the master violinist Guru Nabin Sharma, believes only Classical Hindustani music is worthy. Encouraged by her friends, she tells him at dinner, and he refuses. When her parents come to a rehearsal, Nabin is moved by the performance and offers the group the music room; Leela reminds Shruti that her father himself defied his family of vocalists to play the violin, and Nabin admits he underestimated the power of their own music. The unit also contains the poem 'A Friend Found in Music' by Bryanna T. Perkins.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Identifying stringed instruments, choosing an instrument to play, and whether children and elders differ in their choice of music.
Completing a paragraph with phrases such as 'bite the bullet', 'come around' and 'lost in his thoughts', and discussing literal and figurative meanings.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning

subsections.title: Twin Melodies
points: In Iqbal's room the group finishes rehearsing an Indo-Western fusion piece; Iqbal reads a newspaper review praising Shruti's performance with her father.

Her friends urge her to speak to him, and she promises to 'bite the bullet' and bring it up at dinner.

subsections.title: Twin Melodies
points: At dinner Shruti tells her father about a group Indo-Western fusion concert next week.
Nabin refuses: his rule is one performance every six months, an orchestra drowns individual style, and fusion shows a loss of musicality; he mocks 'phoo' music and leaves.
Leela scolds Shruti for hiding the practice, and Shruti promises not to hide things again.

subsections.title: Twin Melodies
points: At Iqbal's house Shruti plans to practise one last time; her parents enter during the rehearsal and Nabin taps his feet and claps with pride.
Nabin praises the soulful performance and offers the group the music room for practice.
Leela reveals that Nabin went against his family of vocalists to take up the violin; Nabin admits his fears were baseless — 'each bay, its own wind' — and will root for the group.

chapters.title: Carrier of Words
chapters.overview: A profile of Khetaram, a Gramin Dak Sewak and the sole postman of Somarad Branch Post Office in the Thar desert near the Indo-Pakistan border. For fifteen years he has carried mail on foot across burning sand to remote hamlets, read and written letters for villagers, and destroyed letters bearing news of death after reading them aloud outside the house. The piece explains the role of Gramin Dak Sewaks in India Post, the trust rural people place in the post office, and pays tribute to people like Khetaram. The unit also contains the poem 'Words' by Charles Swain.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Discussing pictures of people in the same profession, their difficulties and effect on people.
How words can be 'carried', who could be a carrier of words, and means of staying connected.
Placing words such as slumped, dunes, defying, hamlets, signals and devoid in a passage about a desert visit.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: Part I: Beyond the last railhead and road, Gramin Dak Sewaks are the sole link between remote communities and their families.

Khetaram, his left shoulder slumped from carrying a mailbag, has for 15 years been the sole postman of Somarad Branch Post Office, 2.5 km from the Indo-Pakistan border, 120 km beyond the railhead at Barmer.

He walks through sand too soft for bicycles, delivering mail within 24 hours of dispatch from Jodhpur, with a load that may not exceed 28 kilos, in heat recorded as 49.9 degrees even when it crosses 50.

Since 2001 delivery agents have been accepted as Gramin Dak Sewaks, more than half of India Post's workforce, serving Ladakh, Lakshadweep and the riverine northeast; India Post grew from 25,000 post offices in 1947 to over a lakh and a half.
Part II: GDS must have another livelihood, work five hours a day and may serve till 65; for Khetaram, whose one crop of bajra cannot feed his family, the job gave a new lease of life.

Villagers trust him to read and write their letters; he dreads letters with a torn corner bearing news of death, which he reads outside twice and tears up. He awaits phone lines to become a Gramin Sanchar Sewak — 'Main tayyar hoon'.

chapters.title: Follow That Dream
chapters.author: Irene Chua
chapters.overview: A letter dated 19 June 1995 from Irene Chua's collection 'My Daughter, My Friend', in which a mother encourages her teenage daughter Ming to follow her dream. She explains that greatness comes from effort and sacrifice, that world-class standard needs about ten years of intense pursuit, and that one should count the costs before plunging in. She notes that many people's dreams remain wishes or are changed by circumstances, that life itself may change a person's dreams, and shares that publishing her book is a dream she has chased for ten years. The unit also contains the poem 'Believe in Yourself' by Robert Langley.

sections.title: Reflect and Respond
points: Questions on one's dream, who inspires it, qualities needed, and Abdul Kalam's saying that a dream is 'something that does not let you sleep'.
The role of parents and community in helping children achieve dreams, and a web chart on why it is important to follow a dream.

sections.title: Reading for Meaning
points: Introduces the letter from 'My Daughter, My Friend' by Irene Chua, celebrating the bond between a mother and her teenage daughter Ming.
'By all means follow that dream': great people pursue their dream till it comes true, and reaching world-class standard needs at least ten years of singular, intensive pursuit.
A dream starts with passion, then conviction; count the cost in effort, money and sacrifice, and if it still burns in your blood, plunge; winners depend on a support network.
For many, dreams remain wishful thinking, traded for security or changed by circumstances such as the Japanese invasion in World War II or supporting siblings.
Life itself may change a person's dreams; publishing this book is a dream she has chased for ten years, and she wishes at least one of Ming's dreams comes true.
